title: Learn by Doing: Memory, Buses and CPU Components
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then the past questions on address bus width and memory technology, worked and then taught from nothing.
intro: Part A is the objective questions on this topic, the largest group in the bank after pipelining. Part B is past questions only: address bus sizing and DRAM against SRAM, both from the 2020/2021 paper, both still exactly the kind of question the objective half asks.

lockin.big: "n address lines address 2 to the power n locations. What each location holds is a separate question."
lockin.sub: SRAM is fast, large and needs no refresh, so it is cache. DRAM is dense, cheap and must be refreshed, so it is main memory.

methodFrames.teach: The address bus decides how much memory can be reached: n lines address 2n locations. Everything else in this topic is that one equation rearranged.
methodFrames.ask: A processor has 18 address lines. How many locations can it address?

methodFrames.teach: Keep the powers of two in your head: 210 is 1K, 220 is 1M, 230 is 1G. So 218 is 28 times 210, which is 256K.
methodFrames.ask: Now the half most answers skip. Is 256K locations the same as 256 KB of memory?

methodFrames.check: Only if each location holds one byte.
methodFrames.teach: That is the distinction: byte addressable means one address per byte; word addressable means one address per word. With 4 byte words, 256K locations is 1 MB of storage.
methodFrames.ask: Reverse it. A machine supports 4 GB, word addressable, with 32 bit words. How many address lines?

methodFrames.check: 4 GB divided by 4 bytes is 1G words, so 2<sup>30</sup>, which is 30 lines.
methodFrames.teach: Method in three steps every time: total bytes, divide by the bytes per addressable unit, then take the power of two. Write those three steps down and the marks follow even if the arithmetic slips.
methodFrames.ask: The data bus is separate. What does its width decide?

methodFrames.check: How many bits move in one transfer.
methodFrames.teach: Address bus width decides HOW MUCH memory; data bus width decides HOW FAST it moves. The control bus carries read, write and timing signals. Three buses, three jobs, and the objective half asks for exactly that.
methodFrames.ask: Last: why is cache built from SRAM and main memory from DRAM?

methodFrames.check: SRAM is faster but bigger and dearer per bit; DRAM is dense and cheap but must be refreshed.
methodFrames.teach: Four differences to quote: SRAM uses flip flops and needs no refresh, DRAM uses a capacitor and must be refreshed thousands of times a second; SRAM is faster; DRAM is denser and cheaper per bit; SRAM therefore sits in cache and DRAM in main memory.

questions.heading: 2020/2021, Q1(a)

scenario.text: a. Minicomputers in the eighties had 18 address signals and 18-bit address bus. Answer the following questions: 3mks i. What was the address space of these computers? ii. What may have been the largest possible memory of these computers in bytes if the memory location is 1 Byte? iii) How long should the program counter (PC) of these computers be?

questions.asked: This question repeats. The same question, address bus width against addressable memory, was also set in 2020/2021 Q5(a). Wording and numbers move; the method does not.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
Given 18 address signals, which is the same thing as an 18-bit address bus, and (from the wording of part ii only) one byte per memory location.

Asked three separate quantities. (i) the address space, which is a count of locations, not a size in bytes. (ii) the largest memory in bytes. (iii) "How long should the program counter (PC) of these computers be?", meaning its width in bits.

Marks 3mks for all three sub-items together, so one mark each. That is one line of working per item, not an essay.

Taught in this unit, Module Two Unit 1.

Trap (i) and (ii) look like the same question and are not. The address space is a count of locations; the memory size is that count times the bytes in a location. They agree here only because the paper quietly sets a location to 1 byte, inside part (ii).

exam.problem: Answer 2020/2021 Q1(a) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Given k = 18 address lines · 1 byte per location
Find (i) the address space, (ii) the maximum memory in bytes, (iii) the width of the PC
Formula address space = 2k · capacity = 2k × bytes per location · PC width = k
what each symbol means k = the number of address lines, that is the address-bus width in bits · 2k = how many distinct locations those lines can name · the PC must be able to hold any address, so it is exactly k bits wide
  1. Address space = 2number of lines = 218 = 262 144 locations. 218 = 210 × 28 = 1024 × 256.
  2. At one byte per location that is 262 144 bytes = 256 KB.
  3. The PC must hold any address, so it is as wide as the address bus: 18 bits.
(i) 218 = 262 144 locations. (ii) 262 144 bytes = 256 KB. (iii) PC length = 18 bits.

Now redo it: address space is always 2 to the power of the number of address lines, and the PC is always as wide as an address.

questions.heading: 2020/2021, Q5(a)

scenario.text: a. i) A processor can support a maximum memory of 4GB where the memory is word addressable (a word = 2 bytes). Determine the number of bits required to uniquely address the entire memory. 2mks

questions.asked: This question repeats. The same question, address bus width against addressable memory, was also set in 2020/2021 Q1(a). Wording and numbers move; the method does not.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
Given a maximum memory of 4GB, word addressable, with a word of 2 bytes.

Asked "the number of bits required to uniquely address the entire memory". The word uniquely is the instruction to count addressable units, and the addressable unit here is the word.

Marks 2mks, so two steps: turn the capacity into a count of words, then take the base 2 logarithm.

Taught in this unit, Module Two Unit 1.

Trap answering 32. That is the count of bytes. Word addressable means each address names a 2-byte word, so divide before you take the log.

exam.problem: Answer 2020/2021 Q5(a) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Given memory = 4 GB · word size = 2 bytes · addressing = word-addressable (each address names a word, not a byte)
Find k, the number of address bits needed
Formula N = total bytes / bytes per addressable unit, then k = log2N
what each symbol means N = the number of addressable units, here words not bytes · k = address bits · the phrase word-addressable is the whole question: divide the byte total by the word size before taking the log
  1. 4 GB = 4 × 230 bytes = 232 bytes.
  2. Word-addressable means each address names a word, not a byte. Number of words = 232 bytes ÷ 2 bytes = 231 words.
  3. To address 231 words needs 31 bits (because 231 words need 31 address lines).
4 GB ÷ 2-byte word = 231 words, so 31 address bits are needed.

Now redo it: the trap is word-addressable versus byte- addressable. Divide the total bytes by the bytes per addressable unit first, then take the log base 2.

questions.heading: 2020/2021, Q5(b)

scenario.text: b. i) List four (4) differences between DRAM and SRAM? 4mks

questions.asked: Set once, in 2020/2021. It is still the examiner's own question, and the method behind it is on the syllabus.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
Given nothing. This is straight recall, and it is the cheapest mark on the paper if you have the table memorised.

Asked "List", so a list. Each line must be a difference, which means both sides named on one property.

Marks 4mks for four differences, one mark each. A fifth earns nothing, a third loses one.

Taught in this unit, the Teach box directly above.

Trap writing four statements about DRAM alone. A difference needs DRAM and SRAM contrasted in the same line, so set it out as pairs.

exam.problem: Answer 2020/2021 Q5(b) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Dynamic RAM (DRAM)Static RAM (SRAM)
Stores a bit as charge on a capacitorStores a bit in a transistor latch
Must be refreshed periodicallyNeeds no refresh while powered
Slower accessFaster access
Higher density, cheaper per bitLower density, dearer per bit
Used for main memoryUsed for cache memory

Now redo it: the four you must have are refresh, speed, density and cost. The memory hook: DRAM is Dense, Dynamic (needs refresh) and cheap; SRAM is Static (no refresh), Speedy and costly.
